Along with other architecture components, different sequence embedding strategies were tried such as recurrent layers and convolutional layers. It was found that there exist specific NN components that yield significantly better performing models. Furthermore, Mimic significantly outperformed prevailing standard NNs, Bichrom and DeepSTARR, in modelling protein-DNA interactions and enhancer activity, respectively. This study provides a framework for more extensive studies toward a general prescription of NN architecture for modelling genomics data.

items.title: An improved CRISPR-LICHT screen of 120 Tdark genes illuminates new biologically relevant SOX2 targets in human brain organoids
items.abstract_or_text: SOX2 is a transcription factor and central regulator of neural progenitor identity, yet the downstream molecular networks through which it supports human brain development remain incompletely characterized. Here, we applied CRISPR-lineage tracing at cellular resolution in heterogeneous tissue (CRISPR-LICHT) to human cerebral organoids to functionally interrogate SOX2-dependent regulatory networks. Using a SOX2-focused library targeting SOX2 together with conserved neurodevelopmental regulators expressed in neural progenitor cells, we showed that CRISPR-LICHT detects reproducible lineage- depletion phenotypes across genes already known to be involved in progenitor maintenance, fate specification, glial differentiation and neuronal maturation. This extends the application of CRISPR-LICHT beyond the severe neural progenitor phenotypes previously characterized for microcephaly-associated genes and demonstrates its ability to detect perturbation effects across a broader set of neurodevelopmental regulators, involving SOX2 targets previously defined in mouse and now open to further understanding in a human model setting. We further screened 120 evolutionarily conserved, poorly characterized SOX2-dependent genes classified as Tdark within the Illuminating the Druggable Genome framework and identified 28 candidate hits whose disruption impaired neural progenitor lineage expansion and/or survival. These candidates included proteins associated with cytoskeletal organization, membrane dynamics and intracellular architecture, suggesting that SOX2-dependent developmental programmes may engage cellular processes beyond transcriptional regulation. Individual downregulation of CDC42EP4, a poorly characterized CDC42 effector linked to cytoskeletal organization, revealed altered distribution of targeted progenitors between ventricular- and subventricular- like compartments, with changes consistent with altered progenitor-state progression. Together, these findings expand the functional landscape of SOX2-dependent regulation in human neural progenitors and identify cellular architecture as a potential component of SOX2-associated developmental programs.

items.title: Evaluating Bayesian deep learning for robust biomedical time-series classification under distribution shift: A sleep scoring case study
items.abstract_or_text: In biomedical time-series classification, machine learning models often suffer from deteriorating accuracy and calibration due to distribution shift. We investigate to what degree Bayesian-inspired deep learning improves robustness through Bayesian model averaging (BMA). Using rodent sleep scoring as a case study, we evaluate BMA under distribution shifts in genotype, laboratory, and species. We systematically compare nine approximate inference methods spanning single- and multi-basin approaches across two neural network backbones on in-distribution (ID) data and five out-of-distribution (OOD) datasets. In our results, multi-basin methods perform best, outperforming baselines and single-basin methods. Compared with point estimates, BMA generally improves OOD accuracy and calibration across both architectures, while yielding only modest ID gains. It also often improves selective prediction and OOD and artifact detection, but, interestingly, not inter-rater disagreement detection.

items.title: Limb-localized induction of regeneration reshapes brain and amputation-site transcriptional states in adult Xenopus laevis
items.abstract_or_text: Limb regeneration requires coordinated tissue reconstruction and nervous system reintegration, yet whether regenerative induction alters brain responses to limb loss remains unclear. We analyzed transcriptomics from the paired brains and amputation sites of adult Xenopus laevis after hindlimb amputation with or without a 24 hour exposure to localized, pro-regenerative multi-drug treatment (MDT) delivered through a wearable bioreactor device. At 24 hours post treatment (24 HPT), MDT brains showed increased vascular and basement membrane transcripts and enrichment of oxidative phosphorylation and mTORC1 programs. In the limb, an exploratory integrated stress response (ISR) score increased at 11 and 24 HPT and returned to control levels by 7 days post-treatment (7 DPT), coinciding with induction of growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15), a cytokine responsive to mitochondrial stress. We detected no corresponding increase in brain ISR score. At 7 DPT, MDT brains showed enrichment of immune, heme metabolism and biosynthetic programs, reduced synaptic transmission gene expression, and increased gdf15.L. Relative to an external uninjured reference, MDT and amputation only brains showed concordant changes, with treatment modifying selected programs. Cross-species comparative analyses identified partial overlap with an axolotl regenerative glutamatergic signature and separation from selected mammalian injury profiles. These findings reveal cross-tissue responses to regenerative induction and identify candidate mechanisms of brain body communication in biomedically engineered vertebrate limb regeneration.

items.title: Chromosome-scale nuclear and mitochondrial genome assemblies reveal extreme genome compartmentalization in the hazelnut pathogen Anisogramma anomala
items.abstract_or_text: Anisogramma anomala is an obligate biotrophic ascomycete and the causal agent of Eastern filbert blight, the most economically important disease of hazelnut in the United States. Here, we generated a chromosome-scale reference genome for A. anomala isolate OR-Ennis-d and characterized its nuclear and mitochondrial genome architecture. The 344-Mb nuclear genome was resolved into 9 predicted chromosomes and is repeat-rich, with transposable elements comprising 88.8% of the assembly. Although transposable elements are abundant, their divergence landscape and low retention of conserved protein domains support a history of past extensive transposon proliferation followed by widespread degeneration. Repeat accumulation was highly uneven and generated pronounced genome compartmentalization. Approximately half of predicted genes occur in compact, TE-poor regions with short flanking intergenic regions that are enriched for conserved BUSCO orthologs. In contrast, genes in TE-rich, gene-sparse regions with long flanking intergenic regions are enriched for carbohydrate-active enzymes, secreted proteins, and candidate secreted effector proteins, consistent with a two-speed-like genome architecture. The 462-kb mitochondrial genome is among the largest reported for ascomycetes and contains 117 introns, including an intron adjacent to cob codon 143 that may prevent acquisition of the p.G143A substitution associated with resistance to quinone outside inhibitor fungicides. Finally, we identified mitochondrial DNA insertions at 20 nuclear loci totaling at least 616.9 kb, an unusually extensive amount for a fungal genome. This chromosome-scale genome resource reveals the extreme nuclear and mitochondrial genome architecture in A. anomala and provides a foundation for investigating genome evolution and adaptation to hazelnut resistance.

items.title: Design of full-length agonist and antagonist antibodies for hard targets
items.abstract_or_text: Therapeutic antibodies have transformed modern medicine, yet conventional discovery relies on lengthy experimental workflows, offers limited control over how antibodies engage their targets, and struggles to deliver candidates across many important target classes. Despite recent advances in computational protein design, generating full-length antibodies with desired functional activity and favorable developability profiles remains challenging. Here we present an end-to-end computational design pipeline built around Pythia-1, an all-atom generative model that reasons jointly over amino acid sequence and three-dimensional atomic structure under explicit design constraints. We generated candidates in full-length human immunoglobulin G (IgG) format across 22 therapeutic targets spanning receptor ectodomains, cytokines, growth factors, and G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), a particularly challenging target class for antibody discovery. Following a single computational design round, experimental screening of at most 48 candidates per target identified antibodies with single-digit nanomolar affinities for soluble proteins and single-digit nanomolar cell-binding EC50 values for GPCRs. The pipeline's ability to target specified epitopes and conformational states enabled the design of antibodies with agonist and antagonist activity. In vitro characterization demonstrated target-specific engagement and potent functional modulation, with single-digit nanomolar inhibitory potency in functional assays for a range of targets, including multiple GPCRs. To our knowledge, this study provides the first demonstration of both GPCR agonism and antagonism by de novo designed full-length IgG antibodies. We incorporated key developability and manufacturability requirements into the initial designs by conditioning generation on human germline frameworks and applying sequence constraints to limit known liabilities. The resulting antibody designs exhibited biophysical profiles comparable to or better than those of clinical-stage therapeutic controls. We provide the complete sequences of all lead candidates to support independent experimental validation and further development. Together, these findings demonstrate that our technology can deliver antibodies with programmable function and key properties expected of lead candidates, opening opportunities for first-in-class therapeutics against hard-to-drug targets.

items.title: SynthEHR-DP: Clinically Valid Electronic Health Record Synthesis with Differential Privacy Guarantees
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Background: The sharing of Electronic Health Records (EHRs) for secondary research is severely constrained by privacy legislation and the risk of patient re-identification. Synthetic EHR generation offers a promising alternative, yet existing approaches either sacrifice clinical fidelity or fail to provide formal privacy guarantees. Methods: SynthEHR-DP is proposed: a generative framework combining a Mixed-Type Encoder (MTE), a Temporal Transformer Encoder (TTE), and a Conditional Variational Autoencoder (CVAE) trained under Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD) with R´enyi Differential Privacy (RDP) accounting. A post-hoc Clinical Constraint Layer (CCL) enforces ontological validity via SNOMED-CT rules without consuming any privacy budget. Evaluation is conducted on MIMIC-IV (N ≈ 40,000) and eICU (N ≈ 200,000) at a total privacy budget of (ε= 8, δ= 10 −5 ). Results: SynthEHR-DP achieves near-random-chance membership inference resistance (AUC = 0.52) while attaining a downstream ML utility (TSTR AUROC = 0.786) within 4.2% of non-private baselines and a Clinical Validity Score of 0.961—the highest among all DP-aware baselines. Conclusions: SynthEHR-DP establishes a new state-of-the-art on the privacy utility Pareto frontier for EHR synthesis, enabling safe, open sharing of synthetic clinical data with provable patient privacy guarantees.

items.title: Reversible Pseudonymisation of Documents Sent to External LLMs: an Open Bilingual Benchmark and an Engine
items.abstract_or_text: Professionals send working documents to external large language models. A common safeguard is reversible pseudonymisation: personal data are replaced with placeholders before the request and restored locally in the answer. We present an open benchmark of five existing open tools and a regular-expression baseline on Russian and UK English, and an open engine built on the two strongest tools. The benchmark excludes each tool's own authors' dataset from its verdict, compares the engine with each tool on identical datasets for detection, reports masking precision, and tests on a held-out set of synthetic documents whose files, hashes, decision rules, run plan and stopping rule were published before any run. Two local LLMs test whether placeholders survive. All evaluation data are synthetic, and the benchmark was run by the author of the engine; code, data, predictions and raw answers are released. On external datasets no existing tool meets all predefined thresholds: in UK English the identifier and leak thresholds are not met, in Russian the identifier threshold is borderline. On the last held-out set of 1,000 documents per language, the best existing tools leave a whole value visible in 61% (Russian) and 58% (UK) of documents. On these documents, from the generator it was developed on, the engine does so in 0.3% [0.1; 0.9] and 0.2% [0.1; 0.7], leaves any part of a value visible in 0.8% and 0.2%, and meets all detection thresholds in both languages. In UK English it also restores at least 99% of its placeholders after 760 answers. In Russian it restores only 94.6% [93.6; 95.6] of name placeholders, against a 99% threshold, mainly because the inflection it borrows from pii-guard produces wrong surname forms. The engine was developed over six earlier held-out sets from the same generator; real documents were not tested.

items.title: Data Governance for Generative and Agentic AI : Technology, Law, Economics, and Security
items.abstract_or_text: This book develops a unified governance framework for systems that retrieve, generate, infer, remember and act on information from large language models and retrieval augmented pipelines to autonomous multi agent systems. Eleven chapters and eight appendices integrate three disciplinary lenses-technology, law and economics-across the full lifecycle: data quality, lineage and provenance; global data protection law and intellectual property; the economics of data governance; digital trust, cybersecurity and zero-trust architecture; ethics and responsible AI; governing generative AI pipelines; governing agentic AI and multi-agent systems; data governance in elections and the public sphere; AI regulation across six jurisdictions; and the design of a governance control plane for 2030. Each chapter is anchored in Indian law and institutions while maintaining a comparative, cross jurisdictional perspective.

items.title: HERCULES: a deep-learning framework for RNA-binding region localization and mutation-effect prediction
items.abstract_or_text: RNA-binding proteins regulate essential steps of RNA metabolism, yet identifying RNA-interacting regions and prioritizing sequence variants that alter binding remain challenging from protein sequence alone. Here we present catRAPID signature 2.0 HERCULES (Hybrid framEwoRk for RNA-binding domain loCalization and mUtation anaLysis using physicochemical and languagE modelS), an approach combining a fine-tuned ProteinBERT model with residue-level physicochemical descriptors to predict global RNA-binding propensity, localize interaction sites and estimate the impact of amino acid substitutions. The language model captures domain-scale sequence context, whereas the physicochemical module provides sensitivity to local residue changes. On an independent benchmark, HERCULES discriminates RBPs from non-RBPs with an AUROC of 0.86. At residue resolution, it enriches high-scoring positions within annotated interaction regions across canonical, non-canonical and putative domain classes, while maintaining strong performance on an independent InterPro benchmark. Protein microarray experiments using disease-associated repeat RNAs (CGG, CAG and interrupted CAACAG repeats) independently support multiple non-catalogued candidate RBPs prioritized by HERCULES. Using curated UniProt variants associated with impaired RNA binding, HERCULES also prioritizes deleterious substitutions from predicted changes in binding propensity. By integrating protein-level classification, residue localization, variant-effect prediction and experimental validation, HERCULES provides an interpretable framework for prioritizing RNA-binding proteins, interaction regions and mutation-sensitive sites. HERCULES is freely available at https://tools.tartaglialab.com/hercules and as an open-source Python package at https://github.com/tartaglialabIIT/hercules.git.

items.title: Cell-type resolved prenylomics in mouse liver enabled by a low-input proteomics workflow
items.abstract_or_text: Protein prenylation is a lipid modification crucial for membrane association and cellular signaling, but its dysregulation is linked to cancer and neurodegenerative diseases. Typical "prenylomic" workflows rely on metabolic labeling with bio-orthogonal isoprenoid probes followed by streptavidin enrichment; however, they generally require milligram-scale protein inputs (15-25 million cells), preventing the study of scarce primary or sorted cell populations. To overcome this limitation, we developed a highly sensitive, low-input prenylomic workflow combining optimized streptavidin enrichment with library-free data-independent acquisition (DIA) mass spectrometry. This method enables deep prenylomic coverage from just 50 ug of total protein input, a 20-fold reduction compared to prior methods. In COS7 cells, this workflow identified 91 prenylated protein groups, outperforming TMT-DDA methods that yielded 81 groups from 2 mg of input, using the same bio-orthogonal probe for enrichment, while coefficient of variation (CV) analysis demonstrated superior quantitative precision and reproducibility. Applied in vivo in mice following subcutaneous probe administration, the low-input methodology overcame sample input limitations to profile cell-type-specific prenylomes from dissociated liver tissue, identifying 29 enriched prenylated proteins in hepatocytes and 18 in macrophages. Pathway enrichment analysis showed that the identified proteins are consistent with the biology of the respective cell-types. This robust methodology significantly lowers the sample threshold for lipid proteomics, expanding the accessibility of prenylomics to limited primary cells and sorted tissue populations to study cell-type-specific prenylation dynamics in disease contexts.

items.title: Integrating Metabolic Networks into Hybrid Bioprocess Models
items.abstract_or_text: The optimization and control of bioprocesses require robust in silico models that can accurately capture the complex and dynamic behavior of living cells. While hybrid models that combine machine learning with mechanistic equations have emerged as a powerful tools, they often require relatively large datasets and might yield inconsistent predictions that violate the stoichiometry of metabolism. In this study, we introduce FBA-Hyb, a multi-scale hybrid modeling framework that tightly integrates genome-scale metabolic networks via flux balance analysis (FBA) into its architecture. In our FBA-Hyb framework, artificial neural networks predict key FBA inputs (substrate uptake rates and FBA objectives) while a surrogate FBA module translates them into the metabolic fluxes that govern the bioprocess. A key novelty is that the FBA optimization step is replaced by a surrogate generated with symbolic regression, which encapsulates the FBA model into a compact analytical expression. This allows easy backpropagation through the integration of the neural controlled differential equation based FBA-Hyb bioprocess model. We validated FBA-Hyb against a standard hybrid model (Std-Hyb) using two Escherichia coli fed-batch case studies. In the first study, FBA-Hyb achieved a 42% average improvement in predictive accuracy (R2) during a leave-one-process-out cross validation. Crucially, FBA-Hyb maintains strict stoichiometric feasibility even during extrapolation. Meanwhile, an alternative approach based on standard architectures leads to stoichiometrically inconsistent solutions in 22% of the cases analyzed. In the second case study, we demonstrate how FBA-Hyb effectively simulates unmeasured chemical species and discovers a metabolic shift in sulfate-limited regimes during bioprocessing. By providing a modular, biologically consistent, and computationally efficient architecture, FBA-Hyb offers a robust foundation for the next generation of bioprocess models and sustainable process optimization.

items.title: BurnCare: A deep learning framework for burn injury assessment and TBSA estimation.
items.abstract_or_text: Background: Burn injuries disproportionately affect resource-limited settings. India alone reports over seven million burn injuries annually against only 67 dedicated burn centres. Consequently, initial assessments, such as total burn surface area (%TBSA), which directly influence fluid resuscitation and referral decisions, are frequently performed by non-specialist staff, with known inter-observer variability. Existing computer-assisted tools either require manual annotation on a generic 3D body model or estimate %TBSA using an anatomical approximation (the Rule of Nines) rather than from the patient's own segmented body area. Methods: We developed BurnCare, a deployable artificial intelligence-assisted web and Android-based platform that estimates %TBSA from a single smartphone photograph. The pipeline was developed as a two-stage deep learning system that first isolated the patient from the background (ResNet50 encoder, U-Net decoder) and then segmented the burn skin within that region (DenseNet169 encoder, U-Net decoder), with both stages trained on a prospectively collected, multi-device dataset from a tertiary burn centre in India. The platform supports %TBSA estimation both with scale calibration (using a surgical tape of known length) and without it. %TBSA estimated using BurnCare was compared with independent, blinded estimates from three healthcare professionals for 16 patient photographs, using Pearson's correlation coefficient, mean absolute error (MAE), root mean squared error (RMSE) and the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). Results: The background-removal and burn-segmentation models achieved strong performance (intersection over union 0.9811 and 0.8504, respectively). BurnCare's automatic %TBSA estimate correlated strongly with the mean of three clinicians' estimates (r = 0.746, p < 0.001, MAE = 6.29, RMSE = 8.63 percentage points; n = 16), improving to r = 0.853 (MAE = 4.32, RMSE = 6.37) after manual mask correction; the ICC among the three clinicians alone was 0.728. Conclusions: A two-stage artificial intelligence-assisted platform, BurnCare, was developed. The platform supports burn detection and %TBSA using deep learning models trained on real-world patient datasets. The foreground prediction is supported by a hybrid ResNet50-U-Net, while burn skin prediction is supported by a DenseNet169-U-Net. BurnCare's %TBSA estimates agree with clinical judgement about as closely as clinicians agree with each other, supporting its use as a decision-support and documentation tool for burn triage in resource-limited settings. The dataset collected and the BurnCare platform are available online.

items.title: EvoRouter: Cost-Efficient Multi-Agent Routing via Insight-Guided On-Policy Distillation
items.abstract_or_text: Serving web queries at scale with multi-agent systems requires jointly configuring large language models, collaboration modes, agent counts, interaction rounds, and skills. However, the resulting configuration space grows combinatorially, while sparse execution rewards provide limited fine-grained supervision for interdependent planning decisions. We propose EvoRouter, a self-evolving multi-agent routing framework driven by insight-guided on-policy distillation. A dedicated expert periodically synthesizes performance-cost feedback from configuration trajectories across tasks into reusable conditional routing insights about capability requirements, returns from resource scaling, and interactions among configuration choices. A privileged teacher combines these evolving insights with current execution feedback to provide dense token-level supervision for the router's own planning trajectories through on-policy distillation. Cost-aware reinforcement learning jointly optimizes task performance and computational cost. Together, these training signals internalize execution insights into the routing policy. The updated policy generates new trajectories that support subsequent insight extraction, forming an execution-driven self-improvement loop. We evaluate EvoRouter on 19 in-domain datasets spanning five domains and two out-of-domain benchmarks. EvoRouter achieves an average in-domain accuracy of 68.69%, outperforming the strongest routing baseline by 7.23 percentage points while reducing inference compute cost by 50.95%. Our code is open-sourced at https://github.com/CenYangtze/EvoRouter.

items.title: Bern Sleep-Wake Registry: temporal extraction of comorbidities from unstructured clinical text using a large language model
items.abstract_or_text: Introduction: Large language models (LLMs) may enable the extraction of clinically relevant information from unstructured electronic health records, but most previous work focused on identifying diagnoses without preserving their temporal context. We evaluated the ability of an LLM to extract diagnoses and associated dates from longitudinal clinical reports. Methods In an observational study using the Bern Sleep-Wake Registry, diagnostic annotations from 248 patients comprising 2343 clinical entries were analyzed. Six common comorbidity groups, subdivided into 32 hierarchical diagnostic categories, were evaluated. Using gpt-oss-20b, we extracted diagnosis presence, the number of diagnostic instances, and dates per instance. A reference standard was established through independent review by two physicians, with disagreements adjudicated by a third physician. LLM performance was assessed using diagnostic classification and temporal agreement. Direct annotation costs were compared. Results At the patient level, the LLM achieved an overall F1 score of 0.88 for diagnosis presence and 0.96 for the presence of a reported date. For the earliest reported diagnosis date, agreement with the reference standard was 86.73% at the day level. When considering the cumulative set of dates for each diagnosis, date recall was 87.63%, the extra-date rate was 20.88%, and full agreement was achieved in 58.19% of cases. Human annotators showed substantial disagreement in temporal annotation, with a date recall of 75.49%, an extra-date rate of 17.89%, and full agreement in 58.64% of cases. LLM-based extraction reduced direct annotation costs by 94.65%. Conclusions LLMs can extract diagnoses and their dates from heterogeneous clinical text with high agreement with an adjudicated reference standard. These findings support the scalable use of LLMs for longitudinal clinical registries.

items.title: Scoring the NIH Stroke Scale from bedside exam transcripts: a synthetic benchmark of a decision model and a large language model
items.abstract_or_text: Background. Clinicians score the NIH Stroke Scale (NIHSS) at the bedside, often under time pressure, and ambient AI tools that listen to clinical encounters are now entering practice. It is not known whether software can score the NIHSS from the exam conversation itself, rather than extract a score that has already been written in a note. Methods. We created 112 synthetic code-stroke cases. One hundred were allocated in proportion to real code-stroke presentations, and 12 stress cases tested special scoring rules. For each case, a large language model (Claude Opus 5.5) wrote a reference score form (the answer key) and a speech-to-text-style exam transcript, with main-set transcripts split evenly between a narrated and a telegraphic examiner style. A second model (Claude Fable 5.1), blind to the key, scored every transcript and agreed with the key on 99.2% of items. Each transcript was then scored by Jev, a decision model, and by gpt-6-luna, a general large language model (LLM). The primary outcome was item-level accuracy against the key. Results. The LLM scored 99.0% of items correctly (95% CI 98.4-99.4) and Jev 94.4% (93.2-95.4; McNemar p < 0.001), with exact totals in 101 and 63 of 112 cases. Jev was faster (median 0.15 vs 5.78 s per exam) and cheaper (USD 0.23 vs 0.67 per 1,000 exams). With telegraphic examiners, accuracy fell from 98.0% to 90.9% for Jev and from 100% to 97.7% for the LLM. In a post-hoc analysis that kept only the examiner's words, accuracy stayed high when the examiner narrated (Jev 96.9%, LLM 98.8%) but dropped to about 80% when the examiner used shorthand. Most of Jev's errors fell on four items (language, extinction and neglect, LOC questions and visual fields), and on each it tended to repeat the same mistake, for example scoring slurred speech as aphasia. Its confidence flagged most of these errors. Re-checking the 14.8% of items with confidence below 0.70 would have caught 86% of them, and a simulated hybrid reached 98.8% accuracy. Conclusions. Both engines scored most NIHSS items correctly from exam transcripts. The LLM was more accurate, and the decision model was faster and cheaper, with a confidence signal that could route uncertain items to an LLM. Because the cases and the key are synthetic, these findings need confirmation with recorded exams and human raters.

items.title: Robust enzyme kinetics prediction through pairwise relative learning
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Enzyme kinetics prediction is a fundamental challenge, and numerous computational methods have been developed. However, most methods rely on absolute regression across heterogeneous datasets, which are noisy and prone to regression-to-the-mean bias, limiting accurate identification of highly active enzymes. Here we present DeltaKcat, a siamese neural network framework that reformulates kinetics prediction as a pairwise relative learning problem. By learning pairwise differences within consistent experimental contexts, DeltaKcat improves accuracy, robustness, and generalization over state-of-the-art methods. This framework enables DeltaKcat to (i) mitigate inter-study variability, (ii) generalize to unseen enzymes and substrates, and (iii) prioritize highly active enzymes. We demonstrate these capabilities through systematic benchmarking and external adenylate kinase dataset validation. We anticipate that this approach will be broadly useful for enzyme discovery and engineering, and more generally for learning from noisy biological data.

items.title: An Agentic AI Workflow for Liver Lesion Segmentation and Structured Radiology Reporting
items.abstract_or_text: Despite advances in automated liver lesion segmentation, a gap remains between image-derived predictions and clinically interpretable radiology reports. Bridging this gap requires quantitative measurements that are both reproducible and traceable. We present an evidence-grounded agentic AI framework that connects liver and lesion segmentation with deterministic quantification and structured reporting. TotalSegmentator-based nnU-Net models delineate the liver, Couinaud segments, and lesions, while computational tools extract volumes, dimensions, counts, and anatomical locations. A large language model (LLM) organizes these measurements into a predefined reporting schema, with numerical consistency checks against source measurements. On 51 LiTS cases, the segmentation stage achieved a liver Dice score of 0.947, lesion sensitivity of 75.6%, and positive predictive value of 68.9%. Exploratory screening of 25,494 MERLIN reports identified 10,208 (40.0%) with liver-related abnormalities. By connecting quantitative imaging evidence with agentic report generation, this work takes a step toward human-centered medical AI that prioritizes traceability and clinical relevance.

items.title: GRASP: Group-Adaptive Hybrid RL-SFT Post-Training for Medical VQA without Reasoning Annotations
items.abstract_or_text: Adapting general-purpose vision-language models (VLMs) to medical visual question answering (VQA) is valuable for helping clinicians read images and make diagnoses, but annotated data are scarce and provide only short answers, without reasoning annotations. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) fits these labels but overfits to them and amplifies their biases, eroding out-of-domain (OOD) generalization. Reinforcement learning (RL) better preserves generalization but never uses the gold answer as a training target: GRPO-style algorithms learn from the contrast between correct and incorrect answers within a group of sampled responses, so all-correct or all-wrong groups give no correctness signal. Existing SFT-RL hybrids either apply SFT and RL in separate stages or switch between them per question, or need reasoning traces from experts or stronger models, which medical VQA data lack. We propose GRASP, which combines RL and SFT in every update using only short answers: RL lets the model explore its own reasoning, SFT teaches the gold answer after that reasoning to supply the direct supervision RL lacks, and their balance adapts to how well the model answers each question. Tuning only about 1% of the parameters with LoRA, GRASP outperforms all compared training objectives both in domain and on OOD open-ended questions across Qwen3-VL-8B, InternVL3-8B and Gemma 3-4B. On an OOD benchmark spanning eight imaging modalities, GRASP-trained InternVL3-8B and Qwen3-VL-8B beat all 10 compared general and medical VLMs in open-ended accuracy, including models trained on up to 2,600 times more data or with over 250 times more trainable parameters. We release MedTerse, a dataset of 12.9K short-answer questions, and our code at https://github.com/sea-comet/GRASP-MedVQA.
